claim: Rice dwarf virus (RDV) is transmitted by leafhopper vectors.
source: Rice dwarf virus (RDV), the ﬁrst recorded plant arbovirus transmitted by leafhopper vectors in 1895, causes a severe rice disease in Asia (Wei and Li, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript directly states that RDV is transmitted by leafhopper vectors, citing Wei and Li, 2016.

claim: RDV can be secreted by cultured leafhopper cells via infectious exosomes.
source: We have previously demonstrated that the plant reovirus RDV can be secreted by cultured leafhopper cells via infectious exosomes (Wei et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work (Wei et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2009) demonstrating RDV secretion via exosomes from cultured cells.

claim: RDV hijacks the exosomal release pathway to traverse the apical plasmalemma into saliva-stored salivary cavities.
source: Here, we report that RDV hijacks the exosomal release pathway to traverse the apical plasmalemma into saliva-stored salivary cavities, ultimately moving with exosomes into the phloem of rice plants to establish initial viral infection via leafhopper vectors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as the main finding of the study.

claim: Double-layered RDV particles are approximately 65 nm in diameter.
source: In the cytoplasm of virus-infected type III cells, double-layered RDV particles (approximately 65 nm in diameter) were often engulfed into small vesicles within the MVBs at the periphery of salivary cavities (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript provides a measurement of RDV particle diameter based on electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Virus-free exosomes in salivary cavities measure 53–135 nm in diameter.
source: Virus-free exosomes measured 53–135 nm in diameter, but the packaging of viral particles enlarged exosomes to 110–302 nm in diameter in the salivary cavities (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of exosome diameters from Figure 1K.

claim: Virus-containing exosomes in salivary cavities measure 110–302 nm in diameter.
source: Virus-free exosomes measured 53–135 nm in diameter, but the packaging of viral particles enlarged exosomes to 110–302 nm in diameter in the salivary cavities (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of virus-containing exosome diameters from Figure 1K.

claim: The packaging of viral particles enlarges exosomes in salivary cavities.
source: Virus-free exosomes measured 53–135 nm in diameter, but the packaging of viral particles enlarged exosomes to 110–302 nm in diameter in the salivary cavities (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript compares virus-free and virus-containing exosome sizes, showing enlargement due to viral packaging.

claim: MVBs attach to the cavity plasmalemma and drive the enation of the apical plasmalemma toward the cavity.
source: The attachment of MVBs to the cavity plasmalemma drove the enation of the apical plasmalemma to form a membrane extrusion toward the cavity (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: MVBs fuse with the apical plasmalemma of cavities.
source: This extrusion was followed by the fusion of the apical plasmalemma of cavities with the plasma membrane of MVBs (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Virus-containing small vesicles (exosomes) are released into the salivary cavities.
source: Finally, virus-containing small vesicles (exosomes) were released into the salivary cavities (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: RDV-specific antibody specifically recognizes viral particles within MVBs or exosomes.
source: RDV-specific antibody specifically recognized viral particles within the MVBs or exosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunoelectron microscopy results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: RDV disseminates into salivary cavities by traversing the apical plasmalemma in all types of PSG cells.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that RDV disseminated into the salivary cavities by traversing the apical plasmalemma in all types of PSG cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rab27a is an important regulator of exosome release.
source: Rab27a is an important regulator of exosome release, and the tetraspanin protein CD63 has been described as a key factor in exosomes production (Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Ostrowski et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature (Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Ostrowski et al., 2010) on the role of Rab27a.

claim: CD63 is a key factor in exosome production.
source: Rab27a is an important regulator of exosome release, and the tetraspanin protein CD63 has been described as a key factor in exosomes production (Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Ostrowski et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature (Kalluri and LeBleu, 2020; Ostrowski et al., 2010) on the role of CD63.

evidence: The manuscript describes immunoelectron microscopy results shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Rab27a and CD63 antibodies label some vesicle-like structures in uninfected salivary glands.

claim: Rab27a is colocalized with RDV antigens to form puncta along the cavity plasmalemma or within cavities in virus-infected salivary glands.

claim: Knockdown of Rab27a expression significantly decreases the accumulation levels of RDV P8 in the salivary glands.

claim: dsRab27a treatment significantly decreases the ability of viruliferous leafhoppers to transmit viruses to rice plants.

claim: Double-layered RDV particles are sequestered in endosomal compartments in cultured N. cincticeps cells.

evidence: The manuscript describes electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Endosomal compartments containing RDV form MVBs in the cytoplasm of cultured N. cincticeps cells.

evidence: The manuscript describes electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Virus-containing exosomes are released from infected cultured cells after the fusion of MVBs with the plasma membrane.
